1128.title: Fifth commandment: life and peace (CCC 2258–2317)
1128.hook: respect for every life and the work of peace
1128.howItsDone: Catholics examine themselves on the fifth commandment before confession, including anger and grudges; the sign of peace at Mass, shared before Communion, puts the commandment into a gesture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth commandment: children honor parents, and parents and leaders serve. Your line was honor flows both ways.

Two brothers, at the very start of the Bible's story. One farms, one keeps sheep. Both bring offerings; one is accepted, one isn't, and the older brother's face falls. God warns him that sin is waiting at the door, and that he can master it. He doesn't listen. He invites his brother out into the field, and there he kills him. Then God asks Cain where his brother is, and Cain shrugs: am I my brother's keeper? The fifth commandment begins in that field.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS, TWO OFFERINGS.` → `SIN WAITING AT THE DOOR.` → `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not kill." The Catechism begins with why. Human life is sacred, because from its beginning it involves the creative action of God and stays forever in a special relationship with him. God alone is the Lord of life. In the field, God tells Cain: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me from the earth." Even a life no one else saw taken is heard. Then the Catechism walks through hard ground, carefully. It allows legitimate self-defense, and the duty to protect those in one's care. It teaches that life must be protected from conception, and it rejects euthanasia and suicide, while asking for prayer for those who have died by suicide and saying we should not despair of their salvation. If thoughts of ending your life are close to you, you're not alone: please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Its current text calls the death penalty inadmissible. And it warns about scandal: leading another person to do wrong. Then the commandment reaches inside. Jesus says whoever is angry with his brother is in danger of the judgment; violence starts in the heart. So the section ends with peace, more than the absence of war. It quotes Augustine, peace is the tranquility of order, and calls peace the work of justice and the effect of charity. It lists strict conditions before any war could be called just, and asks everyone to work to avoid war. Cain asked if he was his brother's keeper. In Catholic teaching, the answer is yes: every life, and every peace.
screen: `THOU SHALT NOT KILL.` · `LIFE IS SACRED: GOD ALONE IS ITS LORD.` · `FROM KILLING TO ANGER.` · `PEACE: THE TRANQUILITY OF ORDER.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind with whom something is unsettled: a cold silence, a sharp word, an old grudge. Picture their face without the argument attached, and ask what one small step toward peace would look like. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, wish them well, honestly, once.
Fifth commandment. Thou shalt not kill: respect for every human life, from beginning to end, and the daily work of peace, starting with anger. Today's word.
Your line: every life. Peace starts where anger starts, on the inside. See you tomorrow.

1129.title: Fifth commandment: health (CCC 2288–2301)
1129.hook: care for health, and respect for the dead
1129.howItsDone: Catholics are taught to care for their health with temperance, to accompany the dying with prayer and the sacraments, and to bury the dead with a funeral Mass, a corporal work of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth commandment in Cain's field: every life is sacred, and peace starts with anger. Your line was every life.

Goal reached, ten thousand steps, says the wristband. Down the street, another man hasn't seen a doctor in six years and jokes that his body will let him know. And in an old story from the Bible, a man named Tobit leaves his dinner untasted, goes out, and carries home the body of a murdered man lying in the street, so he can bury him after sunset. Three ways of treating a body, living and dead.
screen: `A WRISTBAND BUZZES.` → `SIX YEARS WITHOUT A DOCTOR.` → `TOBIT LEAVES HIS DINNER.`

segments.voice: The Catechism calls life and physical health precious gifts entrusted to us by God. So we take reasonable care of them, keeping in mind the needs of others and the common good. Society, it adds, should help people find food, clothing, housing, health care, schooling and work. Health is never only private. Then a sharp turn. Morality respects bodily life but doesn't make it an absolute. The Catechism rejects what it calls a cult of the body: sacrificing everything for it, idolizing physical perfection and success at sports. The body is a gift to care for, not a god to serve. In between sits temperance: avoiding every kind of excess, the abuse of food, alcohol, tobacco or medicine. Those who put others in danger by drunkenness or reckless speed, it says plainly, are gravely guilty, and using drugs, except on strictly medical grounds, is a grave offense. Then it follows the body to the end. The dying should be given attention and care, to live their last moments in dignity and peace, surrounded by prayer. The bodies of the dead must be treated with respect and charity, in faith and hope of the resurrection; burying the dead is a work of mercy. That's Tobit, whose journey you followed in year two, leaving his dinner to carry a dead man home. Organ donation after death can be a noble act, and cremation is permitted, as long as it isn't chosen as a denial of faith in the resurrection. From the gym to the graveside: care for the body, honor it, but don't worship it.
screen: `HEALTH: A GIFT ENTRUSTED.` · `NOT A CULT OF THE BODY.` · `TEMPERANCE: NO EXCESS.` · `THE DEAD, TREATED WITH RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Starting at your feet, move your attention slowly upward and notice each part without judging it: tension, tiredness, hunger, pain. Choose one small, reasonable kindness for your body today: a glass of water, a walk, an early night, the appointment you keep putting off. If you pray, thank God for this body as a gift; if not, thank it plainly for carrying you this far.
Fifth commandment. Respect for life includes reasonable care for health, temperance, and respect for the dying and the dead, without making the body an idol. Today's word.
Your line: care, not worship. Living or dead, the body is owed respect. I'll be here tomorrow.

1130.title: Sixth commandment (CCC 2337–2347)
1130.hook: chastity as integration, the person whole and at peace
1130.howItsDone: Catholics are taught that chastity is for everyone, lived differently by the married, the single and the consecrated; it's supported by prayer, confession, friendship and modesty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth commandment and the body: health as a gift, the dead treated with respect. Your line was care, not worship.

A guitar sits on a stand by the window. Five strings are in tune; one has slipped, just slightly. Play any chord, and the whole thing sounds a little wrong, though it's hard to say why. Tighten that one string, and every chord rings. Nothing was added. Something was brought into agreement with the rest. Today's word can sound like only a no. The Catechism describes it as a kind of tuning.
screen: `FIVE STRINGS IN TUNE.` → `ONE HAS SLIPPED.` → `EVERY CHORD RINGS.`

segments.voice: The commandment in the Douay-Rheims is brief: "Thou shalt not commit adultery." The Catechism reads it widely, and opens with a word that might surprise: chastity. It defines chastity as the successful integration of sexuality within the person, and so the inner unity of a human being in body and spirit. The person, whole. Sexuality, in this teaching, isn't the enemy. It becomes personal and truly human when it's woven into the relationship of one person to another, in the complete and lifelong gift of a man and a woman to each other. Chastity tolerates neither a double life nor duplicity in speech: someone who lives one way in public and another in private isn't whole. The Catechism calls chastity an apprenticeship in self-mastery, a training in human freedom. Either we govern our passions and find peace, or we let them rule us. And it's honest that this is long work: self-mastery is never acquired once and for all. It takes effort at every stage of life, with its own stages and setbacks. It's a virtue, and also a gift, a grace from the Holy Spirit. The last note is the warmest. Chastity blossoms in friendship: a person at peace inside can be a true friend, giving without grabbing. Elsewhere the Catechism adds that every baptized person is called to chastity, each according to their state of life: married, single or consecrated. Like the string on the guitar: not removed, brought into tune.
screen: `THOU SHALT NOT COMMIT ADULTERY.` · `CHASTITY: THE PERSON, WHOLE.` · `NO DOUBLE LIFE.` · `IT BLOSSOMS IN FRIENDSHIP.`

segments.voice: Think of the people you'll see today, at work, on the street, on a screen, and notice how easily a person can shrink to one thing: a body, a job title, an obstacle. Choose one and let them grow back to full size in your mind, someone's child, with a history, hopes, a tired day. If you pray, ask for the grace to see people whole; if not, simply hold that one person, whole, for a moment.
Chastity. The integration of sexuality within the person: body and spirit at one, no double life, a self-mastery that frees a person for friendship and gift. Today's word.
Your line: whole, not divided. Self-mastery takes a lifetime, and grace helps all along the way. Until tomorrow.

1131.title: Seventh commandment (CCC 2401–2449)
1131.hook: don't steal, pay fair wages, share the earth's goods
1131.howItsDone: Catholics are taught to make restitution for what they've taken, to pay and work fairly, and to give to the poor through almsgiving, parish collections and the works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chastity: the person whole, body and spirit in tune, no double life. Your line was whole, not divided.

In the back of a garage, behind the bikes, leans a ladder. It belongs to the neighbor. It was borrowed for one gutter job, a few summers ago, and it has quietly become part of the furniture. Nobody would call it stealing. Nobody would call it giving back, either. In Jericho, a rich tax collector climbs a tree to see Jesus pass, and before the day is over he's promising to pay back fourfold anyone he has cheated. The seventh commandment reaches from the ladder to the tax office.
screen: `A BORROWED LADDER IN THE GARAGE.` → `A TAX COLLECTOR IN A TREE.` → `PAYING IT BACK.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not steal." Four words, and the Catechism builds a whole picture of economic life on them. It starts with creation: God entrusted the earth and its resources to the common stewardship of humanity, and its goods are meant for the whole human race. Private property is legitimate; it secures freedom and dignity and helps people meet their needs. But owning something doesn't cancel that first purpose: what a person owns is held for their family and, in some way, for others too. Then theft, widened. Not only taking what isn't yours, but keeping things lent or found. Fraud in business. Unjust wages. Raising prices by exploiting someone's ignorance or hardship. Work done poorly. Tax evasion. Waste. The ladder in the garage belongs on that list. And it asks for repair: what was taken should be given back. That's Zacchaeus, whom you met up a tree in year one. He tells Jesus he'll give half his goods to the poor and restore fourfold to anyone he has wronged, and Jesus answers that salvation has come to that house. A just wage, the Catechism says, is the legitimate fruit of work; withholding it can be a grave injustice. And it ends with love for the poor, quoting Gregory the Great, in paraphrase: when we give the poor what they need, we aren't giving them what's ours, but returning what's theirs. Theft, here, isn't only a hand in someone's pocket. It's anything that keeps the earth's goods from the people they were made for.
screen: `THE EARTH ENTRUSTED TO ALL.` · `THEFT, WIDENED.` · `ZACCHAEUS PAYS IT BACK.` · `FAIR WAGES, AND THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Think through the people whose work you'll use today, the driver, the server, the cashier, the voice on the help line, and picture one of them clearly, on their long shift. Decide what fair looks like for them, a better tip, a prompt payment, a real thank-you, and if anything borrowed is still in your house, when it goes back. If you pray, ask for a generous hand.
Seventh commandment. Thou shalt not steal: respect for others' goods, fair wages, honest work, repair of what was taken, and the earth's goods shared with all, especially the poor. Today's word.
Your line: goods are for all. Even the ladder in the garage can still go home. That's today.

1132.hook: animals and the earth entrusted to our care

A sister leaves for two weeks of work and hands over a leash and a watering can. Walk the dog morning and night; water the balcony plants every other day. The dog isn't the sitter's, and neither are the plants. But for two weeks, whether they thrive is up to the one holding the leash. A good sitter checks the soil with a finger, notices if the dog stops eating, and never treats the spare key as permission for anything. The Catechism files this under the seventh commandment.
screen: `A LEASH AND A WATERING CAN.` → `THE DOG IS NOT YOURS.` → `TWO WEEKS IN YOUR CARE.`

segments.voice: Year one called creation very good. Now, our part in it. Genesis tells how God placed the man in paradise, in the Douay-Rheims, "to dress it, and to keep it." Two jobs: work it, and guard it. Beside it, the earlier line about dominion, ruling over the fish and the birds, sounds different. Dominion, the Catechism says, is not absolute. It's limited by concern for our neighbors, including the people who come after us, and it asks for a religious respect for the integrity of creation. A steward is the one holding the leash: not the owner, the one entrusted. Then the animals. They are God's creatures, the Catechism says; he surrounds them with his providential care, and by simply being, they bless him and give him glory. So people owe them kindness, as saints like Francis of Assisi and Philip Neri showed. Proverbs puts it in one line: "The just regardeth the lives of his beasts." The hard edges, said plainly: animals may be used for food and clothing, and medical experiments on them are acceptable within reasonable limits, if they help to care for or save human lives. But it is contrary to human dignity to cause animals to suffer or die needlessly. And a balance: it's right to love animals, but not to give them the love owed only to persons, and money spent on them shouldn't come first when people are in need. Stewardship holds two hands open: one for the creature in front of you, one for the neighbor you haven't met yet.

1133.title: Eighth commandment (CCC 2464–2499)
1133.hook: truth, reputation and not spreading faults
1133.howItsDone: Catholics examine themselves on the eighth commandment before confession, asking about lies, rash judgment, calumny and detraction; the Church teaches that harm done to a reputation should be repaired where possible.

segments.voice: Yesterday, stewardship: the earth and its creatures, held in trust. Your line was entrusted.

"Did you hear about Dan?" Five words, and the room leans in. What comes next might even be true. Dan did lose his temper at the meeting. Dan's marriage is in trouble. Nobody is lying. And yet, by the end of lunch, a whole table of people who will never help Dan think a little less of him, and Dan doesn't know it happened. The Catechism has a name for that, and it isn't lying.
screen: `DID YOU HEAR ABOUT DAN?` → `NOBODY IS LYING.` → `DAN DOESN'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: The commandment, from Exodus in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour." A courtroom picture: someone lies, and an innocent person pays. The Catechism calls truthfulness the virtue of being true in deed and word, and of guarding against two-facedness. Then it widens the frame, uncomfortably. It names three sins against a person's reputation. Rash judgment: assuming the worst about someone without enough to go on. Calumny: saying false things that damage them. And detraction: telling someone's real faults to people who didn't know them, without a serious reason. Real faults. Dan really did lose his temper. It still counts as a wrong, because a good name belongs to a person, and you can take it from them with the truth. The Catechism offers a habit for the other side, quoting Ignatius of Loyola: be readier to give a good reading to what a neighbor says than to condemn it, and if the words seem wrong, ask what was meant. When harm is done, it has to be repaired, even if the one who caused it has been forgiven. That can be hard: walking back into the lunchroom to say, I shouldn't have said that about Dan. One more thing. Not everyone has a right to every truth. Some things are kept for love's sake, or for safety, or under a seal, like the confessional. Truth, in this commandment, is not a weapon for whoever wants one.
screen: `NO FALSE WITNESS.` · `RASH JUDGMENT, CALUMNY, DETRACTION.` · `TRUE FAULTS CAN STILL WOUND.` · `THE HARM MUST BE REPAIRED.`

1134.title: Truth and beauty (CCC 2500–2503)
1134.hook: beauty expresses truth; art can raise the soul
1134.howItsDone: In Catholic churches, painting, sculpture, stained glass, music and architecture are meant to point to God, and the Church asks bishops to promote sacred art that serves worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eighth commandment: no false witness, and no spreading of faults, even true ones. Your line was guard reputations.

The Catechism's section on the eighth commandment covers lying, false witness, gossip, oaths and the media. Then, in its closing paragraphs, it turns somewhere unexpected: beauty. The work of artists, and the art made for churches. A commandment about not lying ends with a word about art. Why put truth and beauty in the same room?
screen: `THE END OF THE SECTION ON TRUTH.` → `ARTISTS, AND ART MADE FOR CHURCHES.` → `WHY ART, HERE?`

segments.voice: The Catechism's claim is simple: truth is beautiful in itself. Words are one way truth gets told, but not the only one. Truth can find other forms of expression, above all when what has to be said is beyond words: the depths of the heart, the mystery of God. It draws this from the Book of Wisdom: from the greatness and beauty of created things, their maker can be seen, by comparison. Behind every sunset, in that reading, is an artist. Then it turns to human art: a form of practical wisdom, a gift of the Creator, joining knowledge and skill to give form to the truth of something. A carpenter, a singer and a painter are all doing it. Art resembles God's own work of making, so far as it's inspired by truth and love of creatures. Sacred art, it says, is true and beautiful when its form matches its purpose: to call to mind and glorify, in faith and adoration, the mystery of God. Art like that can draw a person toward prayer, toward the love of God. And bishops get a job: to promote sacred art, and to keep out of churches anything that doesn't serve that purpose. So a church window isn't decoration added after the teaching. In Catholic thinking, it's a way of telling the truth. The week, in brief: every life; care, not worship; whole, not divided; goods are for all; entrusted; guard reputations; and now this.
screen: `TRUTH IS BEAUTIFUL IN ITSELF.` · `THE MAKER SEEN IN WHAT HE MADE.` · `ART JOINS KNOWLEDGE AND SKILL.` · `SACRED ART: FORM MATCHES PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Choose one beautiful thing within reach, a painting on your phone, a photo of a church window, a bowl on the shelf, the light on the wall right now. Don't analyze it; look slowly, the way you'd listen to someone you love, noticing color, then shape, then what it seems to say without words. If you pray, let the looking become thanks; if you don't, just stay with it a while.
